blocks.x: Okay, it's going.

I'm Raymond Lopez. I was born down in New Orleans in November of 1889. 1889? In fact, I was born on Thanksgiving Day. I used to get froze out on my birthday. My mother would say, well, don't worry, we'll have your birthday, Thanksgiving Day. And I fooled around, went to public schools, graduated from the Western Union.
What part of town were you born?
I was born down on Domaine Street.
In the French Quarter?
In the French Quarter, Domaine between Dolphin and Bourbon.
Oh yeah. Did any of your family play music, your father or mother?

My father played music, played the French Opera. Oh, he did. And then he played out that. What instrument? He played cornet. In those days it was cornet, you know. But then they got the big trumpets, you know. Yeah. And so, well, I don't know. I just naturally took to the cornet.

Did your father play much around home? He played regularly then in the French Opera Orchestra. Yeah. Of course, did you hear much music around home or did you go to the French Opera when you were young?
Well, my mother used to grab us and take us way up on the Trois Cent, they used to call it, way up on the third tier, you know.
Yeah.
And the old French Opera was down on Bourbon and Toulouse or somewhere around there. I understand it all burned down.
It burned down 1919, many years ago.

Oh. So, but then, no, it just happened to be in me. I'll tell you. I'll tell you. It was a, when I was working for the Western Union, I joined the Woodmen of the World. The kids, you know. Woodcraft, that's what it was. And then, I said, we need a bugle. So, a policeman out there by the name of Ben McKee. He said, well, I'll get you a bugle if you can play one. I said, well, I'll try it. So, he got me a bugle. And then, I practiced up on it and got a few bugle calls. And that was it. I could play the calls. And next thing you know, he says, well, no, I, a friend of mine brought a coronet, Frank Mead. They're a pretty well-known family in Orleans. Frank and Jim Mead. Frank had a, a, a trumpet. I wanted my old man to make a case for it. An old brass trumpet. So, I'd sneak the thing out, see. Fool around, you know, in the good old summertime and this, that and the other. But it's all about here. So, there was another fellow lived back of us. Freddie Burns. He played a car on that. And Freddie heard me playing one day. He came over and said, hey, I didn't know you could play any. Oh, I don't play. Hi, you want to play a day-go wedding with us? I said, what do you mean, me? Yeah, I said, get a book and a half and all you can eat and drink. I said, well, that ain't bad. It's Saturday night. So, Jesus, we go over there and I knew about five tunes I could remember. And Freddie played clarinet, his brother Charlie played bass, and you and Murray played guitar, and I played trumpet. Didn't have any drums. Little house in the house there. And they swung around there, rapping about the third tune. And the guy getting married said, hey, you want to dance? I was that bad, see? I followed up the whole deal. Oh, really?
You were that bad? Freddie didn't want to tell me I was bad. Yeah.
So, I said, yeah, I don't mind dancing. So, I danced and the first thing, you know, they played along and slow without me. The band sounded good.
Just three pieces, then.

Yeah. Well, they played together, see? I'd never play with them. So, little by little, the first thing, you know, I kept one. Freddie says, well, you learn some tunes. So, about a month later, you come over again. By this time, I'd had the whole repertoire on. Everything popular. I could whistle, and when I could whistle, I could play.
How old were you when you started?
I was about 16. About 16. First, I started when I was a kid around, well, when I got the plaintiff's job, yeah. Yeah.
But before then, I was around nine, ten years old. Did you start right on the car net?
Yeah, that's all, a little brass corner. Did you pick up your father sometime and use it?
Yeah, that's all.
I caught him for doing it, see? Yeah, I bet. Oh, Jesus. I put a dent in it one day, oh, Jesus.
What was your father's name, by the way? Edward. Edward.
Edward. Edward Lopez. And he was quite well known down there, amongst the old timers in those days.
Yeah.

Armand Vesey, Emile Tosseau. So, when I was going to get to the, the Wood Crab Boys had a parade or something one day. And here I am up the line, blowing on my bugle, see? Yeah. And the kids all nicknamed me Tosseau. Tosseau used to have the band out of the Spanish Forge. Oh, that's right, I've heard of that.
Emile Tosseau.

He led the offing for 20, 25 years. So, the nickname me Tosseau, there, see? There he went. Well, Tosseau, he's the last guy I saw with it, one of those things, you know? So, I was Tosseau all the way. So, then, from there on, I got picking up little pieces here and there. Never had no idea what to play with anybody, but just for myself, see?
Had you played on anything else first, like a guitar or drums or anything when you were a kid, or a tin whistle or anything like that? No.

Oh, I had a tin whistle. I could play that however, one of them tin whistles. Oh, yeah. But, it just comes natural to me, you know? Yeah. Nobody showed me the scale, you had to fork a couple of notes, you know? Yeah. But, it just came, I practiced, I wasn't right off the bat, but I... Yeah, sure. Then I got to say, my mother said, take that.

Okay, to answer that, then, do you want to stop? Okay, let's see, you were talking about when you first started on your carnet. Yeah. You told about that Italian wedding. Mm-hmm. And you heard other tunes.
Yeah, and then we... Well, little by little, we got into Miller, Gus Miller and I got into a little string band deal, you know?
Yeah.
Violin, guitar, bass, cornton, clannin'. And we plugged around a little around, first thing you know, we run into... Oh, we're done... I started playing with Jack Lane. Oh, yeah. I know him.
Oh, Jack. He's still well. He is, huh? He's talked about you. We interviewed him.
He's a grand old guy. He still looks well. He is, Jack. Well, I'm glad. No, no, a lot of people didn't give Jack credit. But Jack started, they were one of those guys out.
That's right, I think so too, from when I trained. You betcha.

And I'm the guy I can tell you, because I was one of the guys who started. And everybody around there worked for Jack. Jack made that, it was his life. He had maybe four or five bands going, see? And everybody who wanted a job would see Jack. You get this, no matter who you were away, he could use you. But he was a smart guy with us. Go to his wife, go to his house. What'd you have? Big pot of soup, plate of stew, coffee, anything you want. Always have something on the stove. And many of the day, boy, it felt pretty good.
Yeah, yeah.
So, but really, like I said, they didn't give Jack a lot of these books that they write around in. Nobody touches Jack. And he was really the daddy.
You used to start off with the original Dixieland jazz band, something like that. Yeah, yeah. And they used to get all about the other fellas that came before them.

Well, courses like everything else, they bypass a lot of stuff. The real things, you know. That's right. A lot of people do that. But I don't know. He, uh, then we, uh, played with Bill Gallaty's band.
Oh, yeah.
Ernest Giardini, out at the Tonti dance, dance hall. Then we finally turned up.
Where was that?
On the Tonti dance hall, way back on, uh, they were way back on, on, on St. Peter, and Galois somewhere back in there.
Yeah. I thought maybe it was out at the lake or something, because I heard about some of them played out at the lake.

Oh, man. The lake was, uh, uh, with the place like, Quarellas out at Millenburg. Yeah. And, uh, then there's a couple of spots over in Bucktown. Mm-hmm. And, uh, all along the lake you had camps. Yeah, up in the water.
On the water, yeah.

And there'd be a colored band, and then there'd be a white band, and maybe four more colored bands. All trying to out blast each other, see? So then we let, I last on with, with, with Red, Tom Brown. Mm-hmm. And we, playing around, playing here and playing there, playing the university, we played these, uh, I'd watch these, uh, social column, you know? Who's gonna give a dance, who's, who's getting engaged and all that. You know, I had nothing to do, so I didn't go to work in any place. Tom was a tinsmith.
Yeah.

Miller was a plumber. And, his brother Steve was, uh, he was a tinsmith too. And they all had jobs. I was the only guy that didn't have a job. So I, well, I got to find out, I got to be the manager of the band.
He told me that you used to get all the engagements and manage that he told us that, too.
That's right. So, and then, uh, we're playing, we're advertising the fights at the Orleans Athletic Club.
About how early can you remember any year that that was when you started with Tom Brown and Steve?
That was 19, around 1912. 1912.
Yeah. So you were born, you say, 1889. 89. Yeah. So you were about 20, 23 years old.

Yeah, about then, yeah. And, uh, so we were, we were, we were playing on this wagon up in Down Canal Street. Blasting away. It just went about five o'clock, you know. The fight starts at eight. And there's a couple of guys standing around and listening to us. And one said, one come over here. He says, say, buddy. He said, uh, y'all really plays that stuff. He was a white fellow. See, he talked just like an eagle. And who was it? But Charlie Mack of Swar and Mack. They were at the Orphium that week. The two black crows. Oh, yeah. So, he said, I'd let y'all go north. He said, oh, we're gonna give you. Sure, I said, oh, give me an Orphium. Yeah, we sure. I'll fix it. So, next thing I know, there's a fellow by the name of Joe Gorham. Had a girl by the name of Myrtle Howard, working at the Rosefell, at the Grumwald Hotel then.
Yeah, called Grumwald.
Called the Cave, remember? And, uh, I don't know how old you are, but I imagine you remember those days, because it's been a long time since it's been called the Grumwald.
Um, I haven't lived there that long, but anyway, I remember some old books and pictures after it called that. Yeah, yeah. I remember seeing a lot of pictures.

Theodore Grumwald was the manager, see, the owner, rather. And, uh, so this Wyntle Howard, this beautiful review she had on it. And she was a beautiful dancer. So her manager, might have been her husband, I don't know, he come to me one day. He said he got a, when Sworn Mac went back to Chicago, they put the buzz on to Smiley Carbett. Smiley's going around crazy looking for a band. He had a little gypsy outfit. Uh, Drigo, the gypsy violinist, used to dance around there and smile at the women. You know, the guy, get out of here, you polack, you know. So, and the joint was dying, you know. So, Charlie Mac, he buzzed Smiley and so Smiley sends Joe to go and contact these guys. He said, alright. So Joe called me. He got a hold of us and he, he, he, he fell up a deal for us. And from there on we went. And, oh God. We went to the Lambs and stayed there, jam packed the joint. First we went out there, they want to run us out. Yeah, they didn't want no part of us. And, uh, so it so happened that this, a show called Made in America, it was a Schubert show. It was playing at the Palisade, right at the corner, across from the Lambs. Lambs on Clark Randolph, see.
Yeah.
And, uh.
So it was right in the loop then? In the loop, yeah, right in the loop. I always thought it was maybe up farther north on Clark, on the north side.
No, no, just right in the loop, right opposite the Hotel Sherman.
Oh, sure.
See. And, uh, and City Hall was on the other corner. Who?
The City Hall, the big City Hall, right there. Oh, the City Hall, another club. The City Hall, yeah, sure, that's right, right on.

So Smiley wanted us to get out of town. And he said, oh, you boys ain't right. Yeah, yeah, yeah, that Charlie Mack must have been drunk. I said, I don't know, but we're going to stay, man. We got a contract for six weeks. We're going to stay. Oh, you're going to stay, huh? You're going to have a big cigar in his mind. All right. So we, I go up, I'm walking down Clark Street one day and who I run up at Charlie Mack. He said, what y'all doing? I said, man, what do we know? I said, we downstairs in the Lambs. We're dying. I said, the man's about to put the heat on this. Throw us out. I said, who, Smiley? I said, yeah. He said, you tell Smiley. And I swear there wasn't flies in the joint. Nobody would come in. He said, you tell Smiley. Make the reservation for the whole show tonight. I said, you're kidding? And there were about 75 people in the show, see? Yeah. I said, are you kidding? I know something around there. And the man told me out there before he gets ready. Tell him Charlie Mack says reserve the whole joint for 75 anyhow. And the place sat about 200. So I go down and say, Smiley says, what have you been eating oatmeal again? I said, no. I said, you know Charlie Mack, the two black crows? And so he went to verify it, and sure enough, so they went out and bought some flowers and put them all over the table. And up until 11 o'clock, there wasn't a human in the dark. We blasted in our way. Down comes these show people, and we stayed open until about 6 in the morning. Champagne full of ink water.
And they liked it in that time.

From then on, it was it. We had it made. And that was the first place that I ever know of where they put a cover charge on. Dave Barry, the guy that refereed the Dempsey fight, he was the doorman with the rope across. Because he came down the basement, see? And they put 10 cent cover charge on you. Keep the riffraff out. Now, you know that for a dime? To me, that was a funny thing, because I've been in places since. It cost you 2 and a half to get in.
Yeah, that's no cover charge. Yeah, 10 cents. 10 cents.
And so, and we stayed there. Then, uh...
What year was that? Can you remember? 1915. 1915? Yeah.
May of 1915.
May. May of 1915.

Then we went, then, uh... Everybody wanted us. So finally, Frank Clark of Watterson, Butler & Snyder. The music publishers. He came down with a big hot idea that he had an agent coming in town. Harry Fitzgerald. Big agent. You know, we see Fitz. So Fitz comes down. Oh, he's got it all made for a New York show. Yeah, a New York show. We go to New York to, uh... to John and Jolson's show. A show called Dancing Around. Well, if you know Jolson, you know, he always had fights with these directors, producers, and everything. So we're in New York. Fitz brings us to New York, and then Jolson takes a party. He's gone to Florida. You know, he doesn't want nothing to do at the show. And then, there we are. So we fooled around with Fitz for a long time. Played a big party for Diamond and Jim Brady and the Dollar Sisters. And we played for, oh, up at Healy's, Bustonabies. And then finally, we went into the Low Time. Played about 20, 25 weeks for them. In the meantime, the boys all kind of got... One got a yen for home, see? Cold, snow, that's that and the other. So one by one, they took off. And left Tom Brown and I in New York. And we didn't go to the Union and didn't know anybody. So that was it. So then finally, Tom said, well, Ray, I can't make it. I said, it's really rough. In the meantime, little Gusty Miller, he left the band in Chicago, and he went over there with Bert Kelly. And Larry Shields joined us. And then Shields came up. We knew we'd known Shields down home, so you see. Sure. So all right. Then Shields, he went home. This old man was sick or something. And they caught that boat down at that Morgan Lander. For 19 bucks, they could go home and steer it, see? So he took off. So when Miller's in Chicago, I wired Miller. Asked him if there's anything doing around Chicago. So sure enough, he got in contact with Boy Kelly, and Kelly sent for me.
Did Tom Brown go with you, too?
No, Tom had gone down home.
Oh, he'd already left?

He left, yeah. He left me by myself. Well, yeah, I don't blame him. He was, things were rough. Of course, I had my wife and kid, my oldest boy. And it was getting rough for me. I was shoveling snow in New York. And the sign says, Men wanted to shovel snow. 50 cents an hour on day, 75 cents an hour. I said, give me that night shift. I held that for about four or five nights.
Come on in, yeah. Come on in. I was talking about when you were shoveling snow even. Yeah.
My brother was making it the hard way. So sure enough, I went back to Chicago and joined Bert Kelly. That was another guy on the order, Jack Lane.
Was that Bert Kelly? Was that the stables that he had then? Yeah, that's the stables.
Only I didn't play the stables. Kelly had the orchestra at the Sherman House.
Oh, to say.
Yeah.
Was he a leader?
Yeah, he was a leader.
Oh, he actually was a musician.
Oh, yeah. Oh, he played a beautiful banjo.
Yeah, because I thought maybe he was mostly just a promoter. No, no, no. A nightclub, wasn't he?
No, no, no. Afterwards, he got his own nightclub, see?
Yeah.

Then he quit playing. Yeah. So, then I ran into, we went to a place. He put me down to a place called the Windcliffe Inn. First out to Al Trendy's in Chicago, then down to the Windcliffe Inn. And we had some entertainers on there. Benny Fields, Benny Davis, Jack Salisbury, Charlie Thorpe. And I had the band. And we, it got to be a hot spot too.
Yeah.
So, just, things getting hot, see? So, we, first, you know, a girl by the name of Blossom Silly.
Oh, yes. I remember.

Came to Chicago. And she came down to the joint and she got a lot of room. And these fellas had a marvelous trio. Syncopated trio. You know, they did all kind of, they sang and they broke up the rhythm. It's finger snaps, you know, and hit the collars.
Oh, yeah.

And give it back. Everything but was in rhythm, but perfect. Yeah. See, they got a lot of that and she said, I want you guys some next year. Oh, I'll wear that some more. Baloney, see? But sure enough, next year it comes, she brought us in New York. And tore that palace out of the pieces. And from there on, I kept going. I was with Celia for about four or five years. Then I came to the coast. Joined Abe Lyman.
Oh, yeah.
In those days, the old Sunset Inn was the spot. In the 20s.
Was it up on Sunset?
No, no, on the beach, down in Santa Monica.
Oh, I didn't even know where it was.

Yeah, on Santa Monica. The bus estate, the Anheuser-Busch people, they owned it. It was a great, big, beautiful place. And so Mike Lyman, he leased it. And he put his brother Abe in. And from there we went to the Ambassador Hotel. We were there for about eight years. And we got to making records. Gus was with us. Gus Miller, he was with us. At the Inn and down at the Ambassador.
Oh, yeah.

And we went back to New York two or three times. Came all back. And finally went and got in the theaters playing, playing, playing, well, some of them were Francis and Marcos. But we did all right. I mean, so far as I thought. Then when I wanted to, I decided, I said, well, the kids were growing up. But I put them in school. So I stayed home. And I went with Gus Ahnheim. Gus had a band.
In the Coconut Grove, didn't it?
In the Coconut Grove. And that's when Bing got his start.
Yes, sir.
Aye.
You've got a bad unit in there. Okay, it's going.
What are you?
I might ask you about a few of those questions now. First, how long you were at LAMS in Chicago? About how many months you stayed there or weeks?
It was 16 weeks.
16 weeks.
Yeah. Then they closed the place up to remodel it.
Yeah.
And so they said, now, you guys are on your own. Go take a job somewhere.
Yeah.
So we took some little board of time around there.
Yeah.
Then it seemed like they had a little labor trouble. And we got the wind that the place wouldn't be ready in the fall to open. So we said, let's hope this will take off.
Yeah.
Go on our own.
So we went to New York. I was going to ask just who was in the band when you went up to Chicago first, except for Tom Brown. I'm not sure of Gussie Miller.
Gussie Miller, Tom Brown, Arnold Larkana, Bill Lambert, and myself.
Lambert was the drummer. Yeah.
I just looked at some things. I got the whole setup right there.
Oh. The bunch. Yeah, sure. I'd like to see that. Yeah.
Yeah.
If you stop it, you want to go? No, that's right. Let's run it. I can turn it off.
That's your scrapbook. Yeah. Oh, I lost a trunk, but I had a marvelous scrapbook in it.
Oh, really? I bet you had a lot of pictures.
But this is Bill. This is the guys today. Bill's the drummer. Arnold would play piano. Tom played trombone.
Oh, is Arnold a bass player?
He's a bass player.
And piano.

And piano, yeah. Piano, too. And this is out in the valley. Oh, yeah. There's Guss and I. Yeah, I can see. But I have some other pictures in here. Yeah, when we were young at Skirts. That's about the time we were hitting the ball.
Oh, yeah. Those are nice pictures.
This trombone player. This is Bill Lambert when he was a young kid. Oh, what band? Lambert's band in Atlanta City. That's me.
Oh, yeah.
That's me. That's me.
Oh, yeah. That's me.
This kid wrote Whispering, Johnny Schoenberger. Wrote Whispering? Yeah.
Yeah.
His, uh, Guss on the line.
Mm-hmm.
Yeah, right on the beach. This is on a trip to Europe where we're going with his arm, man. Went to England, France, Germany, Belgium. Holland.
There's another boat, a picture of playing in a boat on the beach. Yeah, Atlanta City, yeah. A little skiff.
Yeah. There's another boat.
Mm-hmm.

That's when I was with Longhands Band. Oh, yeah. Featuring me around there. Mm-hmm. He's going on a studio with Kate Smith. Oh, I was going to say, it looks like Kate Smith. Yeah. Nat Bruslov. It's me sitting right here.
He's sitting there with two trumpets. There are in one trombone.
Yeah.
About a ten-piece band.
Mm-hmm.
What?
This is, this is, uh, one of the first sound pitches made at Universal. Made in California. Made anywhere. Oh, yeah. With a great big movie setback. He called Broadway.
Mm-hmm. On Broadway. Oh, yeah.
It was called Broadway.
Called Broadway. It was Broadway. Yeah. It's a big band, about a twenty-piece band or so. Oh, yeah.
I forget who, who started with me, huh?
Mm-hmm.
This is Thomas Mitchell up here. He was, he was in the, he's in the picture, see?
Yeah.
Glenn Ford, I think, was, was.
Glenn Ford. Mm-hmm.
I had one of you.
Tom Mix. Yeah. Trae, what is that called?
Training Quarters.
Training Quarters. It was supposed to be like a.
Yeah, we went around and take, took a farewell pitch of the, of Lyman's band. You know, made a trailer going to, you know, going, ran this trailer ahead of the band.
Yeah. We were playing. You're all dressed up in the Western costumes. Yeah. Big hats.
Here's Tom. Oh, yeah. Tom Mix. His, on the hands band at the Grove, see?
Oh, yeah. Hollywood Review of Hits.
Mm-hmm.
Let's see, was there Gussie Miller in this? No, Gussie Miller.
He wasn't in there, just you. And, and, and, I, I come home, I left my trumpet home, so. He gave me a fiddle.
Oh, you played the violin. Yeah, I'm playing violin.
Did you ever play violin any at all?
No, never.
It was, I always had to play guitar. My kid plays a beautiful guitar.
Oh, that's right. That's from, uh.
The Sandsworth Canceling Music.
Clipping from the Paper, yeah. Yeah, yeah. Lyman. Of August 1923.
Chris Miller and the Zipkowski.
It's Abe Lyman at the Coconut Grove, yeah. Gus Miller and, yeah. Yeah. Mm-hmm.
Oh, yeah. And that's Abe and Jack.
To Rieman and, and, and, and Tarzan, my, my youngest kid. Mm-hmm. His name is Bert. And the nickname, the Blossom Sealing nickname, Tarzan. It's Abe and Jack Dempsey.
Yeah, Jack Dempsey. Yeah. Jack Dempsey.
There's his Jimson streaming quarters.
Oh, yeah. See, September 29th, 1927. Yeah.
And Abe sent me a picture to my brother's reign. Kate, good luck, your pal, Abe.
Yeah.
I was taking, I think, on the Ambassador grounds.
Yeah, it looks like it might be, yeah. Yeah. It looks like. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. The band, I don't know, forgive me. I was also in the York Palace.
Abe Lyman's orchestra. I see it doesn't give the date, but that was at the Keith's Palace in New York, June 4th of some year. May 3rd of 4th.
It's June 4th, yeah. I think a program is out there.
There's a program, Orpheum Circuit News. Let's see if it gives any date on there. Mm, it ought to. It should be, yeah. But I don't see it.
The week is so-and-so, whatever.
April, April 29th at the Philharmonic, but it doesn't, Auditorium, it doesn't. No. Say just which year. Let's look through for a minute, maybe we'll find the year. Oh, 1924.
Yeah, April 24th.
Yeah, Orpheum Program 1924. Mm-hmm.
Let's see if they were part of the program and the next one. Clinton Sisters, George Diskey, Hungarian Tenet, Sarah Platten.
A little play there.
Yeah, there's a sketch or something.

A little sketch or something. Sarah Platten. Mm-hmm. We'll have an ad from the Brunswick records. Were you on these, Brunswick? Yeah, yeah, yeah. All of these Abe Lyman records like No, No, No, Around. Yeah, yeah. Midnight Rose, Havana, California Blues, I Don't Wanna Cry. Werey Weasel.
That's one of my tunes.
Oh, yeah. You wrote Weary Weasel? Yeah. Bugle Call Rag, Honey Babe.
No, Bugle Call was somebody else, a kid in Chicago.
Yes, I know, I think Pettis and some of the New Orleans Rhythm Kings.
That's right.
With the group with Paul Meraz when they were up there, I believe.
And, uh, nice heart. Is it Joe Brown?
Oh, Joe Brown was Joey Brown. Joey Brown, yeah.
Was on there. Oh, Henry Clastic, arrest me.
Yeah. Yeah.
Oh, Henry Clastic, arrest me.
Mm-hmm.
They get locked up for, they want to get locked up for Christmas Eve, you got nowhere to go
to anything.
Oh, was that it? Yeah. They figured they'd give me a ticket dinner on Christmas Day. See, they offered the bum, the woman, the son-in-law, the girl.
Yeah, then here comes the favorite band of movie land, Abe Lyman. Two years at the Coconut Grove Ambassador Hotel. We saved that eight years.
Mm-hmm.
But whatever it is, we're our first two years there, see?
Yeah. Oh, yeah. It's on the best banjo, composer, one kiss, pick it in. Ray Lopez, composer of Bees Knees, Livery Stable Blues, Honey Baby, Weary Weasel.
Oh, yeah. It's got your features, it says, I'll read it here, so be sure to have it on Ray Lopez, trumpet, composer of Bees Knees, Livery Stable Blues, Honey Baby, Weary Weasel.
John Songweiler, violin, he composed Whistlin', Before You Go to Havana, Tell Me Your Story, Rosemary, Girl in the Gingled Island. Yeah. Charlie Kelly, he composed You Kiss Me. You'll Miss Me, is it?
Yeah, You'll Miss Me. You'll Miss Me, yeah.
And Lyman was on everything.
He composed a lot of them, I guess. He got his name on them.
That's right, so I put his name on him, he wouldn't play them.
Yeah.
Love is Just a Flower, Before You Go I'll Cry For You, Peggy Deer, I Don't Know What You Want to Cry For Me, Havana, Weary Weasel, Applesauce, Mandalay. Yeah.

Oh, yeah, that's the river, there's the program of the Coconut Grove. Yeah. Gorham's Follies, here's the guy who sent us up. Well, Gorham's Follies, yeah. John Gorham. Mm-hmm. Yeah. And they list all the personnel here. Yeah. Gus Arnheim, John Thunberger, George Cayley. Pierce. Pierce, Charlie, is it? Charlie Pierce. Was that a Charlie Pierce from Chicago, I wonder?
No, no, no.
It wasn't the fellow from the...
Yeah, Charlie, Chicago was a penalty player, wasn't it?
I don't remember now, I can't think what he played. He had a band, though.
Yeah, Charlie, he wanted to get his band.
Yeah. And Gus Miller, his sax, Ray Lopez, Cornette, Vic Smith, trombone, Jake Garci. Jake Garci. Mm-hmm. And that was... Yeah.
What a nice show that was, too. Let's see, we go on back here.

I remember. Um...I was wondering about some more of that early music like the Tiger Rag. When was the first time you ever heard that or played that?
Oh, that...about 1910.
And what did they call it? Do you remember?

Tiger Rag. That was it. C.F and B Rag. Yeah. That's right.

Yeah. Put some words to it.
Yeah. That's it. Hold that tongue again. Hold that tongue again. And they did alright too.
Yeah. And you played that with Papa Lane's groups?
Oh, yeah. That's all those guys ever knew. Mm-hmm. That's that kind of stuff there. Been played for 40 years before my time.
Yeah.

And, uh, it was just more hoedown stuff, you know, than anything else. Yeah. And, of course, as the fellas went along, they interpreted a little new tricks into it, and this, that, and the other. I hear some of the bands playing Tiger Rag today. Ooh, you wouldn't recognize it.
Yeah, that's right.
You know, they've got a different tune altogether.

Fancy arrangement to it. That's right. That's right. I don't know what it is, yeah. Um, do you remember some of the other pieces, like, uh, original Dixieland One Step? Yeah. Uh, did that have any other title or anything first?

No, but, uh, but that's a phony too, because that was one of the tunes they played down there, but I don't know, remember what they called it. Of course, they, they took credit for, like, took, for a lot of stuff. Yeah. And more power to them if they could get away with it.
Yeah, because nobody else had copied it. Nobody had copied it.
No, that's right.
That's right. Nobody else had done it, and somebody might as well.
And, and, and their agency, Max Hart, he was a smart cookie. And I guess Max was the guy who instigated the whole deal, because he, because they only had five, but he, he cut them six ways. Oh, yeah.
See?
He, he cut them six or whatever, whatever they made.
So he always got one part of it.
Yeah. And he was smart enough to, to copyright all that stuff with them.
Uh, you remember, um, fidgety feet? Yeah. That's a nice sensation.

And Henry Regis wrote Blue and the Blues. Oh, yeah. That to me, that's, it was the only originals that they'd made. Yeah. Climb off my nose. Yeah. Do you remember many other blues that you ever played, just like, say, the Blues in B-flat or anything like that, just without any title? Did you do much? No.
The Blues? Uh, uh, uh. Yeah.
Like the Tin Roof Blues. Did you ever hear any of that? The Tin, yeah.
No, let's see, Tin Roof. Now that.
Brunis, uh, George Brunis and some of them, Leon Rapolo and Paul Merez first made a record of it up in Chicago. I wondered if you'd heard that before though?

No, no, I don't think so, no. I remember the old Tin Roof was, uh, was an old factory, way out on there, at the end of the Washington Blue Line. Back, way back in town. Now it's all built up. Yeah. And something went wrong.
What line was that, the Washington?
The Blue Line. The Blue Line. They used to call it, they used to run out in the Poison Avenue. They call it the Blue Line.
Blue Line.

They ran out in the Poison Avenue and they wound up at Metairie Ridge. And it passed, it passed this, this big factory. And something happened, so they, some guy got a hold of, held dancers. He was way out. Yeah. He got out there and had dancers and moochered around. Well, in Washington. That's right.
And, uh. Was it past Broad Street or Caper?
Yeah, way, way, way back, way back. Past Hagen Avenue.
Past Hagen Avenue. Oh, yeah.
See, Broad was this Satterhagen Avenue. Yeah. And, uh.
Is Jefferson Davis back there now? Carlton, is it in sort of Carlton?

It was around, it, I guess you might, might call it, no. Carlton didn't come down that far. Didn't come down that far. The Boston, no. Yeah. And, uh, so they, that, I think that could be an original. Mm-hmm. Yeah, probably. With the boys who started it, see. Yeah. It's a good tune, though.
Yeah, I like that. But, uh, I don't suppose.
Um, I was wondering about Mardi Gras parades.
If you remember any special things you did around Mardi Gras time? Oh, yeah. We, we played for the, all these big, uh, social clubs around, you know.

The balls or the parades or what? Yeah, there was the balls and the parade. The parade. The parade and the ball, yeah. Now, the, of course, in the old days, they had the big, uh, Rex, Momus, Cody, uh. Comus.
Comus, yeah, Proteus.

And they had those, those were the, the, the, the, the, the, the, the, the, the, the, the Lanterns. The 12th Night Revelers. And they had all those big balls, see. But then later on, these different social clubs had their balls. And I understand, they, there's about 40 balls in our goals. Yeah. So we got, we got our share. They played down at Washington Tilbury Hall or the Outfield Hall on Camp C. And, uh, the Islander Social Club. Oh, Christ, I can't stick to the name now.
Did you play any of those, uh, big balls that they'd have at the French Opera House? No. You didn't play those?
No, they had, they had, uh, big bands. Yeah. Big orchestras, they, they played big tabloos.
Violins and yeah.
Oh, yeah. They had about a 60-piece orchestra. Put that tablo on first, you know. And then they played nice sedate dances, waltzes, mazookas, foxtrotts and stuff like that, see.
When you were young, did you ever play the quadrilles and...
No, no, we never, no.
Did you ever play many waltzes when you played your dance? Oh, yeah, yeah, yeah.
You played all of them. Oh, they, they all, waltz, always was a waltz. The shardists and the mazookas and those things, quadrilles.
You played all of those? No, I never, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no. But waltzes and the, uh, ragtime?
And the foxtrotts and the ragtime, yeah. They called it the walking dance, which is the one step now, what's they call it the walking dance? Well, the walking dance.
What was the difference between the one step and the two step? Can you explain any of that?
Yeah, well, the one step, you make one step. And the two step, you made two steps.
Like the one step, you, this way. This way, see? Just like you're walking. Yeah.
And the two step was. Oh, yeah.
You started to stop and pause. You pause there with your one. Yeah. Would you say one's a faster tempo than the other? Yeah, it is.
Yeah, one's a fast tempo, like you.
Yeah.
Oh, what's the one. By the sea, by the sea, by the beautiful sea, la, la, la, la, la, la. That's the one step. That's the one step, yeah. Then you say, rock me, you see, in my own turkey room, see?
So the two step would be a slower... A slower dance. Slow it down. I see. I wasn't sure about that. And then the name Foxtrot came in for all of these things.
Yeah, then they called it the Foxtrot. Then they came in with the bunny hug.
Would the two step or the one step be called the Foxtrot mostly? The two step. The two step is the... The Foxtrot. Foxtrot tempo. And the bunny hug and all that. Yeah.
Texas Tommy and... It all came in different categories. Yeah.
Yeah, that's interesting. There's different dance steps. But you did play parades in Mardi Gras Day and all those out on the... Oh, yeah.
Parades from nine till six. And then from eight until two for the ball.
Did you ever play a parade like the Big Rex parade too in those? No, no.
The union had that under control. They tied that up right now.
And the bands like Papa Lane's different groups, they played the other smaller clubs. Yeah, the smaller clubs.
They put on costumes and stuff. Yeah. Dressed like minstrels or something, you know. Yeah. Or clowns.
They still have them, yeah.
It's a big day down there.
Oh, yeah. Oh, God.
And then we'd run into other bands, you know, and there'd be a contest, you know. Yeah. Who could I blow the other? Who could I play the other? And...
Did you ever play any funerals? Yes. For funeral bands?

They played, oh, played, oh, they played, oh, they played, oh, they played, oh, they played narrow my guard to thee, slow, jaggy, you know, muffled drums. Yeah. Just bad to creep along, you know. And then after the funeral, of course the Negroes, they didn't even ramble, it seems. Yeah.

Well, they still have those, the colored organizations like the colored Elks and different ones still put those on, but no white funerals like that. Was that for a certain club that you, an organization that would do that when somebody died? Yeah.

As a rule they didn't. Yeah. But once in a while some of us ate something. The president died, and then they hired Brown's band, Elaine's band. I know one time we, Elaine, he gets a, he gets a, a deal, he's gonna play at the Dolphine Theater. Yeah. Big motion picture comes out, you see. Mm-hmm. I think it was, uh, the life of Christ, or some holy picture, you know.
Mm-hmm.

And, oh yeah, Elaine was a catarct, see, he sold the band, oh yeah. Yeah. A 10-piece band, see. And the son of a guy, we get in there and open up with, oh, Mr. Dream Man, please let me dream some more. And she says, the guy's getting nailed on the cross. Oh! Oh! The man, the man threw the band, they know, they want some beautiful music. Yeah, they hired Papa Lane's band. Oh! Almost a dream man.
Did you finish the, they let you finish the... No! They, out we went.
They stopped you right there.

They got some Italian band. Professor Rosatta. Oh yeah. Oh yeah.
That's good. Yeah. He got his band in there.
Yeah.

That was all of the, yeah.
Slow numbers, huh? Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah, they cut it up, coming back. Yeah, they cut it up, coming back, playing all the jazz numbers. Mm-hmm. Yeah, those were, it's an unusual city.
You don't find that in other cities like that. Yeah, it's a funny thing. It's a, it's a, it's a tune that, it's made for a, it's made for a, it's made for a
hit. Oh yes. Oh yes.
Well, I didn't know him in my day, of course he was up in the country, up around New Iberia
somewhere, I believe, see. Mm-hmm. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. And what's that, when the scenes come marching in. Yeah. Well, that was not when we were down there.

Yeah. Like Al G Fields and Lou Dock Theater.

Yeah, that's right. It's the Orphans.
But there were twin theaters there.
Two or three questions. Yeah, I've seen pictures of them. Yeah.

That's before my time. And this band spread out in a great big circle and played the Memphis blues. Mm-hmm. First time I ever heard the Memphis blues. And the first time I ever heard a big band stop and let a clarinet play take a break.
Right.
And from then on, everybody took breaks in blues. Yeah. But the Memphis blues was the first one. And when they say old man handy, was the daddy he was. Mm-hmm.
Do you remember any of the other early colored bands? There was one famous band, Buddy Bolden.

Buddy Bolden. Well, Buddy Bolden came after my, oh, he was ahead of my time. Buddy Bolden, I think, was in his heyday. One I can remember around, well, heard of him, heard a lot about him. But I think he went insane. Yeah, that's right.
I think in 1907, I think is the date. Yeah. So you were still.
But he was still going in, when I heard of him, around, I heard of him around in 90, before the Spanish American War. Mm-hmm. And, uh. You had only been a kid then.
Yeah, I was a kid.
And I know the, they called for volunteers. And the Negroes volunteered. Mm-hmm. They had a Negro regiment.
In the Spanish American War. Yeah.

And, uh, Buddy Bolden band played for it. He, he, he could blow a loud trumpet. Yeah. He'd hear him above everybody, you know. That's what they say. So they, they marched down to the river at the foot of St. Louis Street. And there was a big transport, see. Mm-hmm. They all got on this transport. And, uh, of course the, a bunch of the soldiers had banjos, guitars, everybody, you know. Yeah. It was a free ride. They're going to Cuba, see. Mm-hmm. Odd dog. They're going to have, they have a time. Somebody told them they had, rum was, ran like water. Mm-hmm. Oh, they're going, they're going there for a picnic.
Yeah.
So the band gets on the boat, man. Oh. The boat pulls out, and the band's playing everything, see. And Buddy Bolden band starts up. Home sweet home.
All right.

And I'm telling you, that was it. More banjos coming over that side of that transport. Over the, over the side the boys went. They couldn't, they just couldn't take it. There were banjos and violins floating on that river for a week.
The fellas jumped over to swim back?
Yeah. Yeah, jumped over, swam, before the boat got too far out in the river.
Mm-hmm.
That home sweet home hit them. Yeah. And I understand that from that day to this, the Army does not allow them to ever play home scene home. Yeah. That was in 1898. You were, you saw that?
Did you? Yeah, I was a kid.
I was, you know, I followed the parade. You followed the parade?
Yeah, yeah.

Every time they had music around, yeah, I was there. But, uh, everybody had more fights, you know, white kids, when it's the colored boys, you know. Yeah. Then we'd run around the block and catch up at the parade again, you know. Oh, you learned through the days.
But that was a funny thing.

But to this day, you never hear a big military band playing home sweet home. And the women with all that shouting and screaming and laughing, they start crying. Screaming and crying, see? Mm-hmm. And the band played home sweet home, that was it. Mm-hmm. The Howard Cuba. The Howard Cuba.
Yeah, he was gonna get home again.
That's right.
Oh, I was gonna ask one of the questions about, um, if there are many more people from New Orleans out here that you can think of, like this Paul DeGroix, did you know him?
Yeah, I knew Paul very well. His brother Johnny's got a, they say, got a very fine band on there.
Well, yes, he's still there.
Now, Johnny plays all the carnival balls. Mm-hmm, yeah.

And, uh, about a year or so ago, they were playing out at, uh, the lake at the Pontchartrain, where Mildenburg used to be, in Eastman Park. Is, uh, Paul DeGroix lives out in Hollywood, I believe. He lives in North Hollywood.
North Hollywood. Yeah, he lives out near Miller's.
Not far from Dussleville.
Yeah, he, Paul's over at the Fox Studios. Mm-hmm. And Paul's a very fine drummer. Yes, I know.
I've never met him, though.
Yeah, very, very fine. Very fine, legitimate drummer. He's a good dance drummer.
He still works as a, uh, is he, uh, quite a bit younger than you, or about the same age now?
The guy looks, he's got, he's got a mop of hair on him. He looks, uh, I, I'll say, I don't know. I, I'm proud in 69. Mm-hmm. I bet that Paul's over 60, 63, something like that.
Yeah, I'm only got it.
The guy looks like he's 40.
Mm-hmm.
Really? He's still got that pep and life and stuff. He jumps around.
Yeah.
Good for a million laughs. Mm-hmm. Yeah, he, he's, apparently. And Johnny, I, I saw Johnny, we were down in 52, and Johnny hasn't changed a day since I knew him.
Mm-hmm.

And I remember when Johnny was playing in the scene of the old, which he was with a little pair of white pants on in front of the big band at the lake. Yeah. Yeah, I remember that. And, uh, I was up to see Paul, the mother, Mrs. Detroit. But Paul gets all the big French up with the big carnival balls now. Yeah. I mean, Johnny does.
Yeah, for Johnny.

Well, he, Johnny is a very fine school musician, see? Mm-hmm. And, well, he had an experience. He came out here, too. So, I got him lined up in the, in the radio station. And, it was just around Thanksgiving time. And, we had, we were all playing for a nice great big dinner. For Johnny, see? Yeah. And, uh, Johnny's all set to open up at this big radio station. And, I three-sheeted him all over the town. What a fine trumpet player was. And, he is. And, uh, there comes the, the Thanksgiving dinner, little Johnny. So, then, the studio calls me. Yeah. He says, hey, what happened to that, that, that kid you, you, from New Orleans, that wizard you're talking about? I said, I want to know. I said, of course, we got a great big Thanksgiving dinner waiting. He's waiting for him. That damn fool went back home.
That's quick, huh? Some of these guys get lonesome. Couldn't, couldn't take it. They're homesick and they can't take it.

So, when, when, when that was, oh, that was, that was before. Paul came on. Uh, they wanted a drummer at the, at the Chinese. And, uh, a versatile drummer because they had put a bottle of show on him, is it? Yeah. And, everybody around town tried for it and couldn't make it. So, I, I heard about the job. And, so, a fellow asked me, he said, do you know any drum? I said, I know it, kid. You could cut that. What do you mean? I don't know, kid, you, the overture was Rhapsody in Blue, you see? Yeah. So, and, and those days the show ran about 10, 12 weeks, see? Same show. So, I get home and there's a letter from Paul. I wonder if they had a job out here. So, I wired him. Come on out. Now, he'd been top, top man around New Orleans and legitimate. Been the orphan for years like he was and all of them. He played the singer theater and all that show music. Yeah. So, he come out. Went down and introduced him to the leader. All right, it was great. So, the guy says, you want to look at the book? So, you want to post on your son with the, you know?
Yeah.

The guy came to me after and said, hey, can this guy pick up that book like that, tell me he knows the show? Don't have to have rehearsal. I said, that's it. You don't have to. All right, now, if the guy follows up the deal, you know? I said, oh, he ain't gonna follow it. So, sure enough. There's an act on the bill called Nothing and Chain. Do a lot of pack balls and moves and the drums got all the cues, you know? Yeah. Paul played the act for 10 years at the offium. So, they opened up, first of all, they opened up with Raps in Blue. Yeah, and the drums are everything. Yeah. And it begins, you see? This leader gets a little. Paul's got the band right in his lap. Other drummers, they're in there but they're weak.
They don't know. They're gonna see what they're gonna do.

Yeah, he's got it right down. And they said, that's it. And that only kid had me. Yeah. And when Nelson and Chain come on, they've been having trouble and trouble and trouble. He kicks the guy in the plat and he whistled. Whooo! Bam! Crash! Singin'. They come up and say, wait, there's something wrong with this band. Look down the corner and there's Paul and he sees him.
Yeah.
And he's got it made.
Yeah, that's good.

And the kid finished out that program and he played all over town. Then, things got slack. So, we finally wind up. I'm broke. Paul's broke. Miller's broke. And, uh, so he gets a job on a gambling boat out in the ocean. Five miles out in the water taxi. Go to work every night.
In a gambling boat. Yeah.
I know that was it. So, finally Paul gets a call to the studio. He's late. He can't make the boat. And the minute he sits into the studio, that's it. And he's been there ever since Fox.
In the Fox studio. That's good. He's doing fine.
Around twelve, fifteen thousand a year contract.
Yeah.
And those studio musicians make out alright. Yeah.
So, then, little by little the gambling boat went down.
That's the sad part of that. Oh, yeah. Yeah. Oh, they're just old halls out there, you know. Yeah. Had roulette tables and dice games on and stuff.
They had a band for dancing and that was just the gimmick.
Well, I was going to ask in reading, when you first learned to play, you didn't really play. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. And when you first learned to play, you didn't read at all then, I guess, did you?
No.
Did you ever have any formal lessons that you ever got a method book or anybody helped you much?

No. I did. I bought a thing called a Howard. Howard, for half a buck. Yeah. I bought it in a little store way down on Royal Street. Some guy had a little music shop down there. Yeah. And I bought that thing. I thought it was something about it.
And then you learned just a little music shop. You're just to read yourself.
Yeah. Nah, I don't read any too well. But I'm blessed with a very fortunate ear I can catch stuff. Yeah.
Yeah. Anybody that's a good ear, they make out better that way than they do.

Just like when with Celie now. She had a colored boy around New York by the name of Bill Beaudry. Bill Beaudry made all her arrangements. He made arrangements for the Ziegfeld, see? And the Dillingham shows. Bill Beaudry made her arrangements for her act. Other than the popular songs that were my act, I had to do what I want with them. But the big introductions and the finales and stuff like that. Yeah. And I sat right there. Of course we played, I learned mine from the piano, see? Charlie played the piano and I'd sit on the alongside and get a load of it. But when you sit in an orchestra pit, it's not sitting in a band. No. You sit in a band, you know, the drums are behind you here on this side and the bass is over here, you know, and the piano's here and you droop around this way and you can hear each other. But you get in a theater pit, that's all lost. Spreads out. The drums were on this end and the bass were on that end and the violins are over there and you don't hear what the clarinet and the flute are playing.
Yeah.
And the trombone and the trumpet, they sit here and you don't hear nothing. In an orchestra or a dance band, you hear everything.
Yeah.

And so we used to open up this thing and I used to wave that hat, you know, and people kept saying, what's going on? Some lady in Boston interviewed me one time. I think she was with the Boston Travelers, a musical critic. And she came backstage, we were playing in Boston. And I used to have carried tin cans and derbies and a little barrel with a skin head on it. You got used for a tom-tom.
Oh yeah.

And I picked that up and it got painted all the gild and diamonds all over it. I'd stand up in it with a spotlight on me and I'd wave that little barrel out to them. So this lady come, she come one morning, she come over and of course she called the hotel and asked me to go for an interview. I said, yeah. So she, all these different props that you use, what are they? I said, I explained, she couldn't get into her head what it were. And you actually get music out of them? And I said, hey, that's something. Yeah. Yeah. Can I see them? I said, we're over the theater. Well, when are you going over the theater? Oh, I go, everybody. If you want to go, take a walk home. So we were looking at the Copa Pass in Boston. Walked over to the Keith's Theater and went backstage. And, oh, she was amazed. She was really astounded. And the funny thing about the, you hear about these kazoos, you know, these guys. Well, I bought my little, yeah, I bought my kid a kazoo, you know. He, I'd sit down and he'd run over the horn once in a while, you know, and the kid would sit down and he wanted to, wanted to play, he was singing through a piece of paper, see. So I went downtown when they asked for us a kazoo, I got him a kazoo. And he can play a kazoo.
Do it, do it, do it, do it.

So while we're playing, I'm playing, and so finally he takes his kazoo and he sticks it in the horn. While I'm playing, I said, now wait, don't do that, no. He was a little chap about two years old. He got a dang thing in the, he said, hey, here's the sound. So I went and got a couple of corks and I got some sealing wax and I sealed these two corks on the side. Yeah. And stuck it in the horn.
I've seen where they sell, they sold them like that for a while.

Yeah, that's me though. Everybody around Chicago's got kazoos. They all copied that from yours. Yeah, then the Trombones put three kazoos together, see. Yeah. They fit in the big bell. And son of a gun, I don't copyright it, I just let it go. You should have patented it, yeah.
And you made a little money out of it maybe.

Sure, well, I, so that, that, that was a kazoo craze, you know. Yeah. But, well, you know, you, being, I was a young fellow, I hadn't had any idea about doing it all that, you know. Well, we're just about out of this tape.

I was going to ask one more question before we quit, if, unless there's something else particularly you wanted to add. I was going to ask if there are any early trumpet players when you first started out that you admired and copied more than any of you? That is not necessarily copied, but I mean, as you heard when you were a boy that you, what was the greatest when you were a kid?
Well, King Oliver was one. Manuel Perez was one.
You remember hearing him play?
Freddie Keppard?
Yeah. Another one? You remember, you heard all those fellows.
Oh, yeah. Uh, of course, Louie, I heard afterwards.
Yeah, he was a young kid. Yeah. Younger than you are. He's only 58 now.

Yeah. Well, Louie came up after Joe went to Chicago, see. And, uh, when Manuel Perez played a sweet trumpet, nice, beautiful trumpet. But Joe could blast as high as the sky, see. Yeah. And Freddie Keppard could do the same. And the white boys, a kid by the name of Emil Christian. Oh, yeah.
He's still there. He's working there. He plays bass, though. He plays bass, yeah. And still plays good trombone, though.
Oh, but he was a high trumpet player.
That's what I heard, yeah.
He was.
The Brunus brothers told me he used to be a good trumpet player. Yeah.
And, uh, now Henny, Henny Brunus was a, uh, Richie Brunus was a good trumpet player.
Yeah, he's still living, doesn't play. No. He's cooked on the boats now.
He is.
Still works. I think he's sick, though, right now.
Now, Henny, Henny was a, uh, halibut trombone player. That's what they say.
George Brunus, the younger brother. Yeah, little Georgie. Said that Henny was the greatest in the family. That's right.

Now, here's the funny thing. I played the Orphan in 1919, see? And I'm going out in the Irish Channel to see some folks. And who's sitting across the street on the box step with his big bare feet was this punk, Georgie. Yeah. Used to play alto. You know, the old man had a spasm band. Used to play around the markets on Sunday morning. Henny, Merritt, Richie, Abby and Georgie. And doublehead the uncle. Played bass. And they'd stand on the corner and play stuff, see? So, to make a long story short, He said, hey, Raymond. You were just a car guy. I said, yeah. Come here. I want to talk to you. So, I come in. His mother comes over to her. His mother said, uh, Raymond, uh, Georgia got a wire from, from, uh, from one of my, uh, Bert Kelly. Who is he? I said, Kelly, yeah. He said, yeah. He offers him 75 dollars a week. Does that mean a week? I said, yeah, sure, 75 dollars. Oh, now. But this thing, you weren't 75. He says, yeah. If Kelly heard about him, he wants him, wants to give him 75, he'll give him 75 dollars a week. I said, what, what, what the hell can you play? I used to play a little peck horn, see? Yeah. He's a trombone player. Yeah. So, sure enough, next thing I know is, uh, little Georges in Chicago.
Chicago, yeah. He went up there in about 1921 or so. Yeah.
And next thing you know, uh, another guy, another time, I'll meet him in Atlantic City. He's with Ted Lewis.
Ted Lewis, yeah. He joined Ted Lewis.
So. Mm-hm. Mm-hm.

segments.title: Opening and Ray Lopez's birth in the French Quarter
segments.summary: Recording starts; Lopez gives his birth date in 1889 and his French Quarter birthplace.

segments.title: Father's cornet and the French Opera
segments.summary: His father played cornet in the French Opera orchestra; his mother took the children to the opera's top tier.

segments.title: Bugle, borrowed trumpet and first Italian wedding gig
segments.summary: He learned bugle calls with the Woodcraft kids, got a trumpet, and sat in badly at an Italian wedding with Freddie Burns's band.

segments.title: Starting age, father's cornet and the Tosseau nickname
segments.summary: He started around 16, had borrowed his father's cornet earlier, was nicknamed after bandleader Emile Tosseau, and taught himself by ear.

segments.title: String band and Jack Laine's bands
segments.summary: He joined Gus Miller's string band, then played for Jack Laine, whom he credits as the father of the white bands, and who fed musicians.

segments.title: Gallaty and Giardina at the Tonti Hall and the lake camps
segments.summary: He played with Bill Gallaty's band at Tonti dance hall, and describes the lakefront camps with competing white and Black bands.

segments.title: Tom Brown's band and managing it, around 1912
segments.summary: He became manager of Tom Brown's band, booking dances and fights at the Orleans Athletic Club.

segments.title: Charlie Mack and Joe Gorham send the band to Chicago
segments.summary: Charlie Mack, hearing the band on a wagon, leads to Joe Gorham booking them at the Grunewald Cave; the group goes to Chicago and the Lambs Cafe.

segments.title: Success at the Lambs Cafe and the first cover charge
segments.summary: With Charlie Mack's reserved show party the Lambs fills up, stays open until dawn, and adds a ten-cent cover charge in May 1915.

segments.title: New York with Fitzgerald, stranded, then Bert Kelly's call
segments.summary: The band goes to New York for a Jolson show and the Low circuit; members drift home, Lopez shovels snow, and Bert Kelly sends for him.

segments.title: Bert Kelly's orchestra at the Sherman House
segments.summary: Lopez clarifies that Kelly led the Sherman House orchestra, played banjo, and later ran his own nightclub.

segments.title: Windcliffe Inn and Blossom Seeley's trio
segments.summary: He led the band at the Windcliffe Inn with entertainers, and Blossom Seeley hired the trio to New York, where he stayed four or five years.

segments.title: Abe Lyman at the Sunset Inn and Ambassador, then Gus Arnheim
segments.summary: On the coast he joined Abe Lyman at Santa Monica's Sunset Inn and the Ambassador, made records, then moved to Gus Arnheim at the Coconut Grove.

segments.title: Tape trouble
segments.summary: A bad connection is noted and the recorder restarted.

segments.title: How long at the Lambs and what followed
segments.summary: The Lambs engagement lasted 16 weeks before closing for remodelling; the band then went to New York.

segments.title: Personnel of the band that went to Chicago
segments.summary: Lopez lists Miller, Tom Brown, Arnold Loyacano and Bill Lambert, and mentions his scrapbook.

segments.title: Scrapbook photos: Lambert, Schoenberger and a European trip
segments.summary: Looking at photos, he identifies Bill Lambert, Johnny Schoenberger who wrote Whispering, Atlantic City and a tour of Europe.

segments.title: Photos from Lyman's film shorts and Hollywood Review
segments.summary: Pictures of Lopez in Lyman's band at a Kate Smith studio, the film Broadway and the Training Quarters trailer.

segments.title: Clippings and photos of Lyman's band, 1923-27
segments.summary: Lopez and the interviewer date photos and clippings from Abe Lyman's Coconut Grove years, including Jack Dempsey and his youngest son.

segments.title: Lyman at Keith's Palace and the 1924 Orpheum program
segments.summary: They work out from a program that Lyman's orchestra played New York and the Orpheum circuit in 1924.

segments.title: Brunswick records and Lopez's compositions with Lyman
segments.summary: An ad lists Lyman's Brunswick records; Lopez says he wrote Weary Weasel and Bees Knees, and that Lyman put his name on everything.

segments.title: Coconut Grove program and Gorham's Follies personnel
segments.summary: Reading a program, they list the Grove band members and discuss a Charlie Pierce.

segments.title: More photos and the Blossom Seeley scrapbook
segments.summary: Further pictures of Wesley Barry, Charlie Pierce, his father and Blossom Seeley's act on the road.

segments.title: Livery Stable Blues publishing and royalties
segments.summary: They look at the music's publisher history, the 1917 copyright, and what Lopez earned or missed from it and Bees Knees.

segments.title: Tiger Rag and its earlier names
segments.summary: Lopez recalls Tiger Rag from about 1910 as Number Two or the CF and B-flat rag, and how it was played.

segments.title: The Original Dixieland Band's credit for tunes
segments.summary: He says the Dixieland band took credit for older tunes, their agent Max Hart copyrighted everything, and only a few pieces were original.

segments.title: Blues and the Tin Roof Blues place
segments.summary: He had not heard the Tin Roof Blues record and describes the old Tin Roof factory out the Washington Blue Line.

segments.title: Mardi Gras balls and social clubs
segments.summary: He describes Carnival krewes and the many social club balls the band played.

segments.title: Opera House balls, waltzes and quadrilles
segments.summary: He did not play the French Opera balls; his band played waltzes, foxtrots and ragtime but not quadrilles.

segments.title: One step, two step and the foxtrot
segments.summary: Lopez explains one step versus two step, tempo, and the later foxtrot, bunny hug and Texas Tommy.

segments.title: Playing Mardi Gras parades and cutting contests
segments.summary: Parade and ball hours, the union's control of the Rex parade, costumes, and contests with other bands.

segments.title: Funeral bands and the dream man story
segments.summary: He describes slow dirges at funerals and the 10-piece band thrown out of a theater for opening with a pop tune.

segments.title: Honey Boy Evans' minstrels and the first Memphis Blues
segments.summary: He first heard a band stop for a clarinet break in the blues at a minstrel show, the Memphis Blues.

segments.title: Buddy Bolden's band and Home Sweet Home in 1898
segments.summary: He tells how Buddy Bolden's band played Home Sweet Home on a Spanish-American War transport and soldiers jumped overboard.

segments.title: Paul DeDroit, Johnny DeDroit and homesick musicians
segments.summary: Lopez talks about Paul and Johnny DeDroit, Johnny's carnival band and a trumpeter who went home before a radio job.

segments.title: Getting Paul DeDroit the Chinese Theatre drum job and Fox studio
segments.summary: He brought Paul out, who impressed on Rhapsody in Blue, then the Fox studio job; also the gambling boat.

segments.title: Learning to read music
segments.summary: He did not read well, bought a method book for fifty cents, and relied on his ear.

segments.title: Theater pit versus dance band with Blossom Seeley
segments.summary: He learned from the piano with Seeley's act and contrasts hearing each other in a band with the spread-out pit.

segments.title: Props, the kazoo mute and the kazoo craze
segments.summary: He used props like a tin barrel and derbies, and invented a kazoo mute for his horn that others copied.

segments.title: Early trumpet players he admired
segments.summary: King Oliver, Manuel Perez, Freddie Keppard and Emil Christian were the trumpet players he heard coming up.

segments.title: The Brunies brothers and George Brunies joining Kelly
segments.summary: Discussing the Brunies family, he recalls George on a doorstep in 1919 and getting offered a job with Bert Kelly, later Ted Lewis.
